# Positive-row capacity minima and exclusion of full-cut rows at stochastic maxima

This note closes a regularity gap in the stochastic capacity maximizer approach. It applies in every d>=2. It does not classify maxima with several full rows and does not prove stochastic containment or OC.

Let Delta_d={xi>=0:sum_(j=0)^d xi_j=1}, with uniform probability measure. For x>=0 put

    F_x(t)=Pr(x dot Xi<=t),
    phi_d(x)=inf_{t>0,F_x(t)>0} t/F_x(t)^(1/d).

A proper cut has min x<t<max x. A full row means all its entries are strictly positive.

## 1. Every proper cut of a nonconstant row is regular

For a nonconstant x and a proper t, F_x(t) is jointly C^1 in x,t. Its derivatives are

    partial_t F=|Delta_d intersect {x dot xi=t}|
                    /(|Delta_d| ||grad_Delta x||)>0,
    partial_(x_j) F=-(partial_t F)b_j,                 (1)

where b is the centroid of the actual section. This includes cuts through vertices or lower-dimensional faces.

Here is an elementary justification. Work in the affine span of the simplex, split coordinates into the old normal direction and its orthogonal complement, and integrate along the old normal. Each fiber is a bounded interval. On relative-interior points of the proper section, the cut lies strictly inside that interval. The exceptional section boundary has zero (d-1)-measure. A small simultaneous perturbation of x,t moves the cut in this fiber by a uniformly bounded linear first-order displacement, with a uniform O(norm perturbation)^2 remainder, because the normal component of x stays bounded away from zero. The difference of captured interval lengths divided by the perturbation is uniformly bounded on a fixed bounded projection. Dominated convergence gives (1) and all directional derivatives, uniformly for directions in a compact set, hence the total derivative.

For continuity, use the same coordinates to parameterize nearby section planes over the fixed old plane. Their indicator functions on the simplex converge almost everywhere, since the limiting section boundary has zero relative measure; their Jacobian and coordinate factors converge uniformly. Dominated convergence gives continuity of the section volume and first moments. Thus the derivatives in (1) are continuous. No general-position assumption has entered.

## 2. A positive row has at most one minimizing threshold

First assume x is positive and nonconstant. A minimizer exists in (min x,max x]. Indeed the ratio tends to infinity as t decreases to min x, is continuous afterward, and equals t beyond max x.

The function f(t)=F_x(t)^(1/d) is concave on [min x,max x]. This follows directly from Brunn--Minkowski applied to the nested convex caps: the weighted sum of two caps is contained in the cap at the weighted threshold.

If two distinct thresholds minimized t/f(t), then on the whole interval between them f(t) would equal c t for some c>0. Concavity gives f(t)>=ct, while minimality gives f(t)<=ct. Choose a nonempty open subinterval avoiding all finitely many vertex heights and lying below max x. There

    F_x(t)=C t^d, C>0.                               (2)

The following recursive divergence identity rules this out without a strict Brunn--Minkowski equality theorem. For any k-dimensional face I of the simplex, let F_I(t) be its normalized captured k-volume, and for a vertex j in I let I\j be its opposite face. Away from vertex heights, the affine tangent field e_j-xi and the divergence theorem give

    F_(I\j)(t)=F_I(t)+(x_j-t)F_I'(t)/k.              (3)

The identity remains valid when the face is fully captured or missed, since both sides are then the same constant. Starting from (2), it yields

    F_I(t)=C (product_(j notin I) x_j) t^(dim I)

on every face, by induction. At a vertex l the left side is its capture indicator, while the right side is the strictly positive constant C product_(j!=l)x_j. Hence every vertex must be captured throughout the interval. This contradicts its proper threshold. Thus two minimizing thresholds are impossible.

If the unique minimizer is proper, Section 1 and the elementary envelope argument show that phi_d is differentiable at x. For clarity, all minimizers for nearby positive rows lie in one compact threshold interval bounded away from their smallest entries; otherwise the ratio would diverge. Any convergent subsequence of such minimizers tends to the unique minimizer at x, by continuity. The two touching-ratio inequalities, with the jointly continuous derivatives from Section 1, then squeeze every difference quotient to the derivative of the ratio at this minimizer. In particular

    partial_j phi_d(x)=F_x(t)^(-1/d)b_j.              (4)

Thus every proper minimum of a positive row is unique, regular, and differentiable; these are conclusions, not extra hypotheses.

## 3. Exactly which positive rows minimize at the full cut

Let m=max_j x_j and suppose the row is not constant. If m occurs r<=d-1 times, the upper tail near m satisfies

    1-F_x(m-delta)=O(delta^(d+1-r))=O(delta^2).

Indeed, with g the smallest positive gap m-x_j, the upper-tail event implies that the sum of the d+1-r nonmaximal barycentric coordinates is less than delta/g. Direct simplex integration bounds its probability by a constant times delta^(d+1-r). Therefore

    (m-delta)/F_x(m-delta)^(1/d)=m-delta+O(delta^2)<m

for small delta>0. The full cut cannot minimize.

If m occurs exactly d times, write the row as (a,m,...,m), 0<a<m. For a<t<=m its lower-tail cap is a vertex simplex and

    F_x(t)=((t-a)/(m-a))^d,
    t/F_x(t)^(1/d)=t(m-a)/(t-a).

This ratio is strictly decreasing, so its unique minimum is the full cut t=m and phi_d(x)=m. For the constant row m1, the minimum is again m, with its atom at the full cut interpreted directly. Consequently these two statuses are the complete list of positive rows without a proper minimum.

## 4. Exact one-sided derivatives at the full-cut status

Let x=(a,m,...,m), 0<a<m, and vary one of the d high coordinates. Set

    beta=(m-a)/m in (0,1), p=d/(d-1).

With the convention that D_- is the derivative of epsilon -> phi_d(x+epsilon e_j) from negative epsilon, the derivatives are

    D_+=1-(d-1)/d beta^(1/(d-1)),
    D_-=1-(d-1)/(d beta)[1-(1-beta)^p].              (5)

Hence the upward derivative jump is

    D_+-D_-=(d-1)/(d beta)
                     [1-beta^p-(1-beta)^p]>0.       (6)

We give the limiting minimization proof to justify (5), including the movement of the optimal threshold. For a bounded perturbation w of the d high entries and epsilon>0, condition on the low barycentric coordinate L. It has density d(1-L)^(d-1); conditionally the normalized high coordinates are uniform on Delta_(d-1), independently of L. Let W be their dot product with w. At t=m+epsilon s the upper-tail condition is exactly

    L<epsilon(W-s)_+/[(m-a)+epsilon W].

For bounded s and sufficiently small epsilon the right side lies in [0,1). Integrating the displayed density gives, uniformly on bounded s,

    1-F_(x+epsilon w)(m+epsilon s)
       =d epsilon E(W-s)_+/(m-a)+O(epsilon^2).

The cap ratio therefore equals

    m+epsilon[s+beta^(-1)E(W-s)_+]+O(epsilon^2).     (7)

No escaping thresholds are omitted. Let L0=max|w_j|. Testing the full cut gives capacity at most m+epsilon L0. For a minimizing threshold t with t+epsilon L0<m, the event inclusion in the unperturbed lower tail gives

    phi_d(x+epsilon w)
       >=t(m-a)/(t+epsilon L0-a).

Together with the preceding upper bound, this forces t>=m-C epsilon for a fixed finite C depending only on a,m,L0. On the other hand t can be taken at most the perturbed maximum, hence t<=m+epsilon L0. If t+epsilon L0>=m the same lower localization is immediate. Thus the normalized minimizing thresholds s stay bounded. Uniformity in (7), and testing each fixed s, prove that the directional derivative is exactly

    min_(s in R) [s+beta^(-1)E(W-s)_+].              (8)

The minimum lies between min W and max W: outside that interval the expression is monotone toward it. It is the mean of the highest beta fraction of W, with fractional allocation at a level if necessary. This last assertion follows by differentiating the convex function in s, or directly by integrating the upper tail.

For a single increasing high coordinate, W=Z has density (d-1)(1-z)^(d-2) on [0,1]. The mean of its highest beta fraction is 1-(d-1)beta^(1/(d-1))/d. For the decreasing direction W=-Z, (8) is minus the mean of the lowest beta fraction of Z; direct integration gives that lower mean as the second line of (5). This proves (5)--(6). Positivity in (6) uses p>1 and 0<beta<1. Varying the low coordinate alone leaves phi=m in a neighborhood, so its derivative jump is zero.

For a constant positive row x=m1, a single-coordinate variation has D_-=0 and D_+=1. For negative epsilon the preceding full-cut formula gives capacity m. For positive epsilon, write the minimizing threshold as m+epsilon s_epsilon, 0<s_epsilon<=1. Necessarily s_epsilon->1: otherwise its captured fraction stays bounded below one while its cap ratio must be at most m+epsilon. Since F<=1, the ratio is at least m+epsilon s_epsilon. This and the full-cut upper bound yield D_+=1.

It follows that at EVERY positive coordinate of EVERY nonnegative row, the two one-sided coordinate derivatives exist and their difference D_+-D_- is nonnegative. A positive row with a proper minimum is C^1 by Section 2. The full-cut cases are covered above. A row with exactly one zero has capacity equal to the geometric mean of the other entries and is smooth when varying a positive coordinate while retaining that zero. A row with at least two zeros retains zero capacity when a positive coordinate is varied. The identically zero row has no positive coordinate to consider.

## 5. Full-cut rows cannot persist at a nontrivial weighted maximum

Let c_i>0 and let X be a global, or merely local, maximizer of sum_i c_i phi_d(X_i) over column-stochastic (d+1)-square matrices. Suppose a full row r has a full-cut minimizing threshold and maximum entry m<1. Choose any of its high coordinates j. Another row i has X_ij>0 because this column has remaining mass 1-m>0.

Transfer epsilon in column j from row i to row r. Both signs are feasible for sufficiently small epsilon. The full-cut row contributes a strictly positive derivative jump by (6), or by the constant-row calculation. The funding row contributes a nonnegative derivative jump: reversing its coordinate direction exchanges and negates the one-sided derivatives, so the jump is unchanged. All other rows are constant. The weighted objective along this line therefore has right derivative strictly greater than its left derivative.

A local maximum would require its right derivative to be at most zero and its left derivative at least zero. The strict opposite ordering is impossible. Thus no such row with m<1 can occur.

If m=1, at least d columns are saturated by that row. Every other row is supported in at most the single remaining column, so its capacity is zero for d>=2. The full row has capacity one. The resulting capacity vector is the unit vector e_r, which belongs to D_d: put one in every off-diagonal entry of row r, and put the remaining diagonal column's mass in any other row. Thus this case is already paid by a zero-diagonal matrix, regardless of the weights.

Consequently, at any positive-weight stochastic capacity maximum whose capacity vector is not an already-paid unit vector, EVERY full row has a unique proper regular minimizing threshold and a differentiable capacity. This holds for all d>=2. It supplies the regularity required by the section-centroid and one-full-row arguments; it does not eliminate multiple full rows.

The restriction d>=2 in the maximum exclusion is essential. For d=1 a nonconstant positive row has phi_1(x)=max x and the single high coordinate is smooth, so the strict jump mechanism is unavailable. The separate d=1 stochastic problem is elementary and is not inferred from this argument.
